pass_a_gloss: [...] and they will march and pass through the desert. As if also a storm of winds should pass through a desert. Raising the dust, and all but confusing everything. And he adds: For fearful is the vision, and a harsh one was announced to me. For very sufficient, even bare and alone, is the sight of the enemies, and the most valiant multitude of the fighting men equipped for war, to make a harsh fear in those who behold. But he says not only to have beheld, but also, It was announced to me, he says; for together with the sight he was taught also the outcome of the affairs, clearly from God. [Lemma, Isaiah 21:2:] The one who sets aside sets aside, and the lawless acts lawlessly. Unrebukable, he says, is the boldness of those coming on. For they are not kindled by human reasonings toward the gentle; nor does anyone of those among them consider any of the fitting things; but he acts lawlessly without restraint, and sets aside according to what seems good to him, no sparing being in him. For they do not look toward mercy, but the work eagerly pursued by them will be, he says, to act lawlessly and to set aside. He said something such also through the voice of the same to the inhabitants of the land of the Assyrians: Behold I bring upon you the Medes, who do not reckon silver nor have need of gold. They will shatter the arrows of young men. For when God brings wrath on those who offend, there will be nothing able to help. But rather a beast-like mind takes up dwelling in those wishing to ravage those against whom they may run. [Lemma, Isaiah 21:2-4:] Upon me the Elamites, and the envoys of the Persians come upon me. Now I will groan and comfort myself. Because of this my loin was filled with faintness, and pangs took me like the woman giving birth; I did wrong so as not to hear, I hastened so as not to see. My heart wanders, and lawlessness immerses me, my soul has been set in fear. The discourse in these [lines] has the force of a putting into character. For the Assyrian is brought in, both fearing the attack and not ignorant of the ranks of the enemies, and against whom the aim of the war is for them. For not against some others, but upon me, he says, the Elamites and the very best of the Persians have set out. I will groan then and comfort myself. For to those who have come into the last misfortune there seems to be present some manner of consolation, to lament and wail. For the tear is squeezed out from pain. And it is a strange thing if Assyrians lament, having always been harsh and arrogant, and with brows raised very much against all the nations, and thinking to have a resistance not easy to meet. But those so bold, and swollen with thoughts beyond man, accept a womanish tear, and prepare a lament over themselves, broken down to weakness before the trial of the war. For my loin was filled with faintness, and pangs took [the section breaks off].

lemmas.gloss: speech put in a character's mouth

pass_b_english: …and they will march on and pass through the desert. “As if a storm of winds should pass through the desert” (Isaiah 21:1), raising the dust and all but throwing everything into confusion.

He adds: “For the vision is fearful, and a harsh one was announced to me” (Isaiah 21:1–2). For the mere sight of the enemy alone, and a most valiant host of fighting men equipped for war, is quite enough to strike harsh fear into those who see it. Yet he does not say only that he saw it, but also, “It was announced to me”; for together with the sight he was taught the outcome of events, plainly by God.

“The one who deals faithlessly deals faithlessly, and the lawless one acts lawlessly” (Isaiah 21:2). The boldness of the attackers, he says, cannot be checked. For no human reasoning kindles them to gentleness; no one among them gives thought to what is right, but each acts lawlessly without restraint and deals faithlessly as he pleases, with no mercy in him. For they do not look to mercy; rather, he says, their whole eager work will be to act lawlessly and faithlessly.

He said something similar through the voice of the same prophet to the inhabitants of the Assyrians' land: “Behold, I am bringing the Medes against you, who do not value silver and have no need of gold. They will shatter the arrows of young men” (Isaiah 13:17–18). For when God brings wrath on those who sin, nothing will be able to help. Rather, a mind like a wild beast's takes up its dwelling in those who are bent on ravaging whomever they rush against.

“The Elamites are upon me, and the envoys of the Persians are coming against me. Now I will groan and comfort myself. Therefore my loins are filled with faintness, and pangs have seized me like a woman in labour. I did wrong so as not to hear; I hastened so as not to see. My heart wanders, and lawlessness plunges me under; my soul is set in fear” (Isaiah 21:2–4).

The words here have the force of a speech put in a character's mouth. For the Assyrian is brought on stage, fearing the assault, well aware of the enemy's ranks and of whom their war is aimed at. “Not against any others,” he says, “but against me the Elamites and the very best of the Persians have set out. So I will groan and comfort myself.”

For those who have fallen into the worst misfortune seem to find some kind of comfort in lamenting and wailing, since pain squeezes out tears. Yet it is a strange thing if the Assyrians lament, since they had always been harsh and arrogant, carried their brows very high against all the nations, and thought themselves hard to stand against.

But those who were so bold, swollen with thoughts beyond what is human, give way to womanish tears and compose a lament over themselves, broken down to weakness before they have even tasted battle. “For my loins are filled with faintness, and pangs have seized…” (Isaiah 21:3)

choices.why: ἀθετέω of breaking faith; Septuagint Isaiah 21:2.
The boldness of the attackers admits no rebuke or restraint.
